ourClaims.studySummary: Site cites 'A 2016 meta-analysis (McLellan et al.)' confirming cognitive benefits at 100-300mg, diminishing returns above 400mg/day.

humanEffects.notes: Site claims most robust effect, reliable across all populations and doses above 75mg.
Site claims particularly effective during sleep deprivation or extended work sessions.
Site claims post-learning caffeine (200mg) may enhance 24-hour memory consolidation.

sideEffects: Anxiety and jitteriness at high doses
Insomnia if taken late in the day
Elevated heart rate in sensitive individuals

howToTake.dosage: 100–200mg for cognitive effects; do not exceed 400mg/day
howToTake.timing: Avoid within 8 hours of bedtime due to 5-6 hour half-life

studies.title: A review of caffeine's effects on cognitive, physical and occupational performance
studies.design: narrative review (McLellan, Caldwell & Lieberman) — this is the site's cited 'McLellan et al. 2016' source; note it is a REVIEW, not a formal meta-analysis as the site's studySummary field labels it
studies.duration: reviews both acute and repeated-dose literature
studies.outcome: alertness, vigilance, attention, reaction time, memory, executive function, physical performance
studies.result: Following low-to-moderate doses, alertness, vigilance, attention and reaction time improve consistently; effects on memory and higher-order executive function (judgment, decision-making) are less consistent. Physical performance benefits emerge above ~200mg (~3mg/kg). Repeated caffeine dosing is an effective strategy to maintain performance during restricted sleep in occupational settings.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Caffeine for the prevention of injuries and errors in shift workers
studies.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (13 RCTs)
studies.population: shift workers / jet-lag simulated conditions, mostly young participants
studies.outcome: errors, cognitive performance by domain (concept formation/reasoning, memory, orientation/attention, perception, verbal function)
studies.result: Caffeine significantly reduced errors vs placebo. Pooled SMDs favored caffeine for memory (SMD=-1.08, 95% CI -2.07 to -0.09), orientation/attention (SMD=-0.55, 95% CI -0.83 to -0.27); effects on concept formation/reasoning and perception were directionally favorable but not statistically significant; no benefit on verbal function/language. High risk of bias noted for allocation concealment and selective outcome reporting across included trials.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Acute caffeine supplementation as a nutrition-based strategy to mitigate sleep-loss-related cognitive and operational performance impairments in military personnel: a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.population: military personnel / military-related populations under sleep deprivation, restriction, or sustained wakefulness
studies.outcome: vigilance/response performance, complex cognitive performance, military task performance
studies.result: Caffeine significantly improved vigilance/response performance (SMD=0.73, 95% CI 0.50-0.96, I²=0%), complex cognitive performance (SMD=0.54, 95% CI 0.16-0.93, I²=0%), and military task performance (SMD=0.45, 95% CI 0.19-0.71, I²=29.2%) vs placebo during sleep loss. Effects most consistent for vigilance/response speed.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Post-study caffeine administration enhances memory consolidation in humans
studies.dose: caffeine administered post-study (inverted U-shaped dose-response identified)
studies.result: Post-study caffeine enhanced performance 24h after administration via an inverted-U dose-response curve; the effect was specific to memory CONSOLIDATION, not retrieval. This is a precise, direct match for the site's specific claim about '200mg post-learning caffeine enhancing 24-hour memory consolidation'.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Caffeine Use in Sport: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Acute Side Effects and Implications for Athlete Health and Safety
studies.design: systematic review and meta-analysis (48 RCTs, 38 in meta-analysis)
studies.outcome: self-reported side effects: headache, abdominal discomfort, tachycardia, insomnia, increased urine output, anxiety, nervousness
studies.result: Caffeine significantly increased odds of headache (LogOR=0.74), abdominal discomfort (LogOR=1.12), tachycardia (LogOR=1.47, >4x higher odds), insomnia (LogOR=1.20), anxiety (LogOR=1.29) and nervousness (LogOR=0.82), all p<0.001, in a dose-dependent manner; doses ≤6mg/kg (~420mg for a 70kg adult) associated with lower side-effect risk than >6mg/kg.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed
studies.duration: single administration at 0, 3, or 6 hours before habitual bedtime
studies.outcome: self-reported and objective (portable sleep monitor) sleep disturbance, total sleep time
studies.result: A 400mg dose taken at bedtime, 3h before, OR 6h before bedtime each significantly disrupted sleep relative to placebo (p<0.05 for all) — even a full 6 hours before bed produced a meaningful reduction in total sleep time.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

verdicts.claim: Alertness & Wakefulness — evidenceStrength strong, magnitude large, 'most robust effect... reliable across all populations and doses above 75mg'
verdicts.reason: Broadly consistent with McLellan 2016's review conclusions and directly quantified by the 2026 military meta-analysis (SMD=0.73 for vigilance/response performance under sleep loss); this is among the best-replicated caffeine effects in the literature.

verdicts.claim: Reaction Time — evidenceStrength strong, magnitude moderate, 'tolerance-resistant'
verdicts.reason: Ker 2010 Cochrane review found caffeine improved orientation/attention performance (SMD=-0.55) and the 2026 military meta-analysis found consistent vigilance/response-time benefits; McLellan 2016 specifically notes reaction time is one of the more tolerance-resistant caffeine effects, matching the site's framing.

verdicts.claim: Sustained Attention — evidenceStrength strong, magnitude moderate, 'particularly effective during sleep deprivation or extended work sessions'
verdicts.reason: This is precisely the population and outcome quantified by the 2026 military sleep-loss meta-analysis (SMD=0.54 for complex cognitive performance, SMD=0.73 for vigilance) and the Cochrane shift-worker review — strong, direct evidence for exactly the sleep-deprivation framing the site uses.

verdicts.claim: Memory Consolidation — evidenceStrength moderate, magnitude small, 'post-learning caffeine (200mg) may enhance 24-hour memory consolidation'
verdicts.reason: This is a precise match to Borota et al. 2014 (Nature Neuroscience), which found post-study caffeine specifically enhanced 24-hour memory consolidation (not retrieval) via an inverted-U dose-response curve — the site's claim is accurately scoped and correctly hedged ('may enhance').

doseAssessment.trialRange: 100-400mg across cognitive/vigilance trials; side-effect meta-analysis found doses >6mg/kg (~420mg for 70kg adult) carry disproportionately higher risk of headache, tachycardia, insomnia and anxiety vs ≤6mg/kg.
doseAssessment.efsaComparison: Site's 100-200mg cognitive dose sits at or below EFSA's verified single-dose threshold of up to 200mg for healthy adults; site's 'do not exceed 400mg/day' matches EFSA's daily intake threshold of up to 400mg for healthy adults exactly. EFSA additionally caps habitual intake at 200mg/day for pregnant women — a limit the site's caffeine page does not mention.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Dose guidance is accurate and matches EFSA 2015 (Scientific Opinion on the Safety of Caffeine, EFSA Journal 2015;13(5):4102). Add an explicit pregnancy caution (≤200mg/day total from all sources) since the site's sideEffects list omits it entirely.

safetySignals.signal: EFSA (2015) Scientific Opinion on the Safety of Caffeine: single dose up to 200mg and daily intake up to 400mg do not raise safety concerns in healthy adults; pregnant women should limit habitual intake to 200mg/day — the site's page does not mention the pregnancy limit at all.

Caffeine significantly increases panic-attack risk in patients with panic disorder (53.9% of PD patients had a panic attack after caffeine vs 1.7% of healthy controls, at doses ~400-750mg) and increases anxiety in both patient and healthy populations at these doses — a clinical population caution the site's sideEffects list only gestures at generically ('anxiety and jitteriness at high doses').

400mg caffeine taken even 6 hours before bedtime significantly disrupts sleep (reduces total sleep time) relative to placebo — stronger and more specific than the site's general '5-6 hour half-life, avoid within 8 hours' framing, but directionally consistent and slightly more conservative than the site's own advice.

gaps: The site labels its McLellan et al. citation a '2016 meta-analysis' in the studySummary field; the actual McLellan 2016 paper is a narrative review, not a formal meta-analysis. Minor citation-accuracy issue worth correcting.
No pregnancy-specific caffeine limit is mentioned anywhere on the site's caffeine page despite this being one of EFSA's headline conclusions (≤200mg/day for pregnant women).

Panic-disorder/anxiety-vulnerable population caution is understated relative to the meta-analytic evidence (Klevebrant 2021) showing a >30-fold relative risk of panic attack in PD patients vs healthy controls at high doses.
